Weed is first seen writing to the Times, which the Legation regards as the amateur's 'invariable mistake'.

essential: The Assistant Secretary offer is declined ('an Assistant Son'). The irregular position yields an 'irregular education'.

Seward sends influential Americans abroad in 1863. Thurlow Weed takes over the press and is first seen writing to the Times; his unselfishness and his playing of men as cards. Adams follows him 'like a little dog'.
The Weed exchange and Adams's later reading of it (values, not principles). Evarts as a contrasting 'economist of morals' who becomes an intimate.

The governing question: did young Adams err in assuming British bad faith? The Legation treats Russell as false while the Minister personally trusts him; there is one student among the many costly tutors.
The Alabama ('No. 290') escapes after Collier's opinion. Russell's later confession of negligence; the real issue was intent, not fault.

Walpole's 1889 life reveals the September 1862 story: Palmerston's conditional letter of 14 September; Russell's Gotha reply of 17 September agreeing to mediation 'with a view to the recognition' and recognition if it failed; Palmerston's wait-and-see answer of 23 September. 'The roles were reversed.' Keep the key Gotha sentences.
Granville's opposition, and his letter naming only Pam, Johnny, Gladstone and perhaps Newcastle; hence 'suspect too much'.

Antietam and the Emancipation Proclamation, then Gladstone's Newcastle speech of 7 October ('made a nation'), reached after deliberate reflection. Adams's harsh moral conclusion at the time (no difference from Napoleon). Palmerston has Lewis repudiate the speech.

Russell calls the Cabinet for 23 October. The 23 October interview: Russell's 'embarrassment' and explanation of Gladstone, and his 'Yes!'. Meanwhile the Cabinet had rejected his proposal that day. Gladstone's rejoinder of 24 October; Napoleon's overture; Gladstone's diary for 11–13 November ('Lord Russell rather turned tail', Palmerston's 'feeble and half-hearted support').
Forty years later Adams reads this 'with stupor', together with John Hay. The summary of how each valuation proved false.

Character conclusions: Russell, thought 'dishonest but strong', is upset by believing himself true; Palmerston proves cautious and honest; Gladstone is the sum of contradictions. Keep the essence of the 1896 confession ('incapacity of viewing subjects all round').
Close: politics cannot stop for psychology; the sum still looks like one will 'as a diminution of a dangerous power'; each student answers for himself alone.
optional: Westbury/Bethell paragraph (para 13): condense to a line or drop.
The Canada sentence of the Gotha letter, and the France/Russia sequencing.
Lyons delaying departure; Punch caricatures of Russell.
The Henry James burning-glass aside and the 'Complex these gentlemen were not' elaboration: compress into one sentence.
Long passages of the Adams despatch quotation (paras 37, 40): paraphrase, but keep the 'embarrassment' and the neutrality assurance.
risks: Dense documentary quotation; paraphrase the despatches and keep only key phrases verbatim.

title: POLITICAL MORALITY (1862)

verbatim.purpose: The central exchange that frames the chapter's question of trust.
verbatim.text: "Then, Mr. Weed, do you think that no politician can be trusted?" Mr. Weed hesitated for a moment; then said in his mild manner: "I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so."
"The world can absorb only doses of truth," he said; "too much would kill it."

verbatim.purpose: The ironic turn after Granville's letter.
verbatim.text: In truth, the Legation knew, then, all that was to be known, and the true fault of education was to suspect too much.

verbatim.purpose: Russell's categorical assurance, which Napoleon's later 'No!' exposes.
verbatim.text: "I asked him if I was to understand that policy as not now to be changed; he said: Yes!"
One's diplomatic education was a long mistake.
The only resolute, vehement, conscientious champion of Russell, Napoleon, and Jefferson Davis was Gladstone.
he was obliged at last to admit himself in error, and to consent in spirit--for by that time he was nearly as dead as any of them--to beg his pardon.

verbatim.purpose: Gladstone's own phrase, which Adams turns back on him here and in the next chapter.
verbatim.text: only a mistake, but one of incredible grossness

voice_profile: Third-person autobiography in which the old Adams ironically judges young 'Henry Adams' or 'the private secretary'. It moves from concrete scene to aphorism ('a friend in power is a friend lost'), deflates itself constantly ('insect', 'worm', 'small fry'), and builds long periodic sentences out of semicolon series and dashes. It returns to the vocabulary of 'education', 'force', 'unity' and 'chaos'. Irony works through reversal: the lesson learned proves wrong, and the evidence arrives forty years too late. The past perspective of 1862 and the retrospect of the 1900s run side by side and must stay clearly distinguished. Quoted documents, such as letters, despatches and diary entries, serve as evidence that ironizes the narrator's certainties.
